title: Why Howard Zinn became a ‘people’s historian’
text:
Why Howard Zinn became a ‘people’s historian’
A new biography connects the dots between the professor’s labor-union beginnings and the left-wing outlook that shaped his bestselling history book.
Howard Zinn achieved a level of fame unthinkable for most historians. His landmark 1980 work, “A People’s History of the United States,” has sold more than 4 million copies. The book was name-checked in the television shows “The Sopranos” and “The Simpsons,” and in the 1997 film “Good Will Hunting.” (“You want to read a real history book?” Matt Damon’s character demands of his mentor, played by Robin Williams. “Read Howard Zinn’s ‘History of the United States.’”) For decades, Zinn traveled the country lecturing to packed auditoriums. Eager listeners waited in long lines for the rumpled professor to sign their books.
Dave Zirin, sports editor at The Nation magazine, witnessed that phenomenon firsthand. In 2008 and 2009, Zirin conducted a series of interviews with the octogenarian in front of large audiences. (Zinn died in 2010.) Now Zirin, who first read “A People’s History” more than 30 years ago, has written an effusive biography of Zinn. “The People’s Historian” explains how the activist-historian, born to poor Jewish immigrants in Brooklyn in 1922, developed the radical beliefs that informed his teaching and his writing.
“A People’s History” famously celebrates those who had been left out of traditional “great man” versions of the American story, including women, wage laborers, and racial and ethnic minorities. With its bottom-up view of history, the book emphasizes the power of grassroots movements to effect social change.
Zirin demonstrates that Zinn’s life story shaped the worldview in “A People’s History of the United States.” After graduating high school in 1940, Zinn found a job as a shipyard worker at the Brooklyn Navy Yard, where he became a union organizer. The demands of the role increased dramatically as the U.S. prepared to enter World War II, and Zinn, according to the author, felt that the workers’ labors “were being fundamentally undervalued.” His experiences as a manual laborer, Zirin notes, “put him on the side of workers in labor disputes throughout his life.”
Eager to join the fight against fascism, Zinn enlisted in 1943. He served as an Air Force bombardier. Weeks before the end of the war, he participated in the intensive bombing raid of Royan, a town in occupied France. Zinn was cited for distinguished service, but he was horrified by the operation’s steep civilian death toll. “Zinn wrestled with what he did in Royan, how his superiors could order the bombing and why he obeyed, for the rest of his life,” the author writes.
A new biography connects the dots between the professor’s labor-union beginnings and the left-wing outlook that shaped his bestselling history book.
After the war, Zinn attended college on the GI Bill. He received a Ph.D. in history from Columbia University, where he focused on the labor movement. By then, he and his wife, Roslyn, had two young children. So he loaded trucks on a night shift while working his way through college and graduate school.
During this period, the Zinns were under FBI surveillance for their involvement with leftist groups that had ties to the Communist Party. Zirin states that Zinn was never an official party member, but his association with radical politics might have been enough to limit his job prospects. Upon completing his Ph.D., he received only one employment offer, from Spelman College, a historically Black women’s school in Atlanta.
Zinn and his family arrived in segregated Atlanta in 1956. The young professor quickly became a favorite of the students (including Alice Walker and Marian Wright Edelman) and a thorn in the side of the college administration. The Zinns made their house available to young people involved in the burgeoning Civil Rights Movement, hosting meetings and strategy sessions. The professor participated in sit-ins and was arrested alongside his students. “He was there for us through thick and thin,” Edelman later recalled.
Zinn, who also advised the young activists of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee during this period, was fired from Spelman in 1963 after continued clashes with the school’s conservative president, who believed that the protests Zinn supported were damaging the institution’s reputation.
His next academic post, at Boston University, where he taught from 1964 to 1988, brought more conflict with leadership. At BU, Zinn was an extremely popular professor. Off campus, he was also developing a high profile due to his vocal opposition to the Vietnam War. (In a trip followed closely by the media, Zinn traveled to Hanoi with Jesuit priest Daniel Berrigan in 1968 to secure the release of three American prisoners of war.) In 1979, he helped head a strike of the university’s faculty, clerical workers, and maintenance workers. BU’s president, John Silber, publicly called his star professor “barbarous,” “uncivilized,” and “contemptible.”
Of course, the runaway success of “A People’s History” also greatly increased Zinn’s profile. But, as Zirin observes, Zinn’s version of the American story was far from universally acclaimed. Its leftist viewpoint was, unsurprisingly, anathema to those on the right. (The book, subtitled “1492-Present,” opens with a portrayal of Christopher Columbus as a violent conqueror.) A number of left-leaning academics criticized the book, too, questioning the seriousness of its scholarship and calling it oversimplified. Zirin, a staunch admirer of his subject from the first page to the last, mounts a robust defense of “A People’s History.” He focuses as much on the book’s effect as on the text itself, emphasizing that it has inspired generations of readers to continue to learn about America’s origins.
Though Zinn’s masterwork is decades old, the debate continues. In 2020, President Donald Trump referred to “propaganda tracts, like those of Howard Zinn, that try to make students ashamed of their own history.” Zirin handily establishes that Zinn’s intention was to make readers feel empowered, not ashamed. “We don’t have to engage in grand, heroic actions to participate in the process of change,” the historian once asserted. “Small acts, when multiplied by millions of people, can transform the world.”
